summary:
Mars Survival Atlas is an interactive Martian map that turns NASA Mars data into survival decisions. Instead of showing only what the surface looks like, it tells a crew whether a place is safe to land, live and travel through.
We combined layers for terrain and slope, water ice, sunlight, hazards and past landing sites into three tools. The Site Scorer gives any point on the map a 0-100 survival score with plain-language reasons. The Route Planner finds the safest path between two points by using slope as travel cost. The Survival Guide Card gives a per-site checklist covering water, power, shelter and hazards.
This answers the challenge by making a Martian map useful as a survival guide, not just a reference image. It matters because Mars data is scattered and hard for non-experts to read, and a wrong site or route choice could cost a mission. A single, clear map helps planners, students and the public understand where humans could realistically survive on Mars.
Before you submit, make sure this matches what you actually built, and name the NASA datasets you used.
details: What it does and how it works Mars Survival Atlas is an interactive Mars map that tells a crew whether a place is safe to land, live and travel through. It combines NASA Mars data layers (terrain, slope, likely water ice, sunlight, hazards, past landing sites). Users click any point to get a 0-100 survival score with plain-language reasons. They can also plan the safest route between two points, with path cost based on slope. Each site gets a survival guide card covering water, power, shelter and hazards. Benefits It turns large, scattered, expert-only data into one clear answer. Planners can compare sites quickly, and students and the public can explore Mars and understand why a place is safe or risky. Intended impact We want to make Mars exploration data easier to understand and use. It could support early mission planning and education, and show how open NASA data can support real survival decisions. Tools and technology Map: Leaflet or CesiumJS with NASA Mars Trek tiles Data processing: Python (numpy, rasterio) for slope and score layers Frontend: HTML, CSS and JavaScript Route planning: A* or Dijkstra on a slope-cost grid Hardware: standard laptops, no special hardware Data: NASA open Mars datasets Creativity Most Mars maps show what the surface looks like. Ours answers "can we survive here?" It packages the answer as a score, a guide card and a safe route, like a survival guide for another planet. Factors we considered Safety first: slope, roughness and hazards weigh most heavily in the score. Survival needs: water ice and sunlight for power. Clarity: results are explained in plain language, not raw numbers. Data limits: we used open data and are open about its resolution and uncertainty. Scope: we focused on a few strong features that work well within the 48-hour hackathon. Our approach We started from the question a crew would ask, picked the data layers that answer it, then built the score, the route planner and the guide cards. We tested them on known landing sites like Curiosity and Perseverance [if you do this] to check the scores made sense.
